title: "Swiss Stats Explorer"

---

```{r, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>", message = FALSE, warning = FALSE)
```

The [Swiss Stats Explorer](https://stats.swiss/) (SSE) is the new data
platform of the BFS. It uses the SDMX standard. It replaces STAT-TAB and its
PXWeb API (see
[Get started](introduction.html#from-stat-tab-to-the-swiss-stats-explorer)).

## Our example: the vacancy rate

In this article, we look at the **vacancy rate**: the share of homes that
are empty and available, in percent. A low vacancy rate means that it is
hard to find a home. We compare three cantons: **Geneva**, **Zurich** and
**Bern**.

The BFS publishes the vacant dwellings every year since 1995, for each
canton, district and commune.

## How it works

A dataset has **dimensions**, for example the canton or the number of rooms.
Each dimension has a list of **values**, for example `GE` for Geneva. You
get data in three steps:

1. Find the dataset with `bfs_sse_datasets()`.
2. See its dimensions and values with `bfs_sse_dimensions()`.
3. Choose the values you need (the `filters`) and download the data with
   `bfs_sse_data()`.

The functions are a thin layer over the API: they send your query, and the
API does the work (for example, it finds the latest version and gives the
labels in your language). So they keep working when the API changes.

```{r}
library(BFS)
library(dplyr)
```

## Step 1: find the dataset

`bfs_sse_datasets()` lists all the datasets. There is one row for each
version of a dataset. Search for "vacant" in the names and the
descriptions:

```{r}
datasets <- bfs_sse_datasets(language = "en")
datasets |>
  filter(grepl("vacant", paste(name, description), ignore.case = TRUE))
```

The description tells you more about a dataset. The first row of a dataset
is its latest version:

```{r}
datasets |>
  filter(dataset == "DF_LWZ_1") |>
  slice(1) |>
  pull(description)
```

The descriptions come as the API gives them, so some have HTML tags, such
as `<br>` for a new line.

The dataset we need is `DF_LWZ_1`. This id is the `dataset` argument of the
other functions.

You can also search on [stats.swiss](https://stats.swiss/). The id of a
dataset is in the URL of its page, after `df[id]=`.

## Step 2: see the dimensions

```{r}
dimensions <- bfs_sse_dimensions("DF_LWZ_1", language = "en")
dimensions
```

There is one row for each value of each dimension:

- `dimension` and `dimension_label`: the id and the name of the dimension.
- `value` and `value_label`: the code and the name of the value.

The dimensions of the dataset:

```{r}
distinct(dimensions, dimension, dimension_label)
```

### Find the codes you need

We need the codes of our three cantons. Search them by their name:

```{r}
filter(dimensions, value_label %in% c("Geneva", "Zurich", "Bern"))
```

Be careful: one name can have several codes. Here, a canton and its main
city have the same name. For example, `ZH` is the canton of Zurich and
`261` is the city of Zurich. We need the cantons: `GE`, `ZH` and `BE`.

### Find all the communes of a canton

The column `parent` gives the value above each value. For the regions, the
parent of a commune is its district, and the parent of a district is its
canton. For example, the city of Zurich (`261`) is in the district `B_112`,
which is in the canton `ZH`:

```{r}
filter(dimensions, value %in% c("261", "B_112", "ZH"))
```

So you can find all the communes of a canton in two steps: first its
districts, then the communes of these districts. The communes of Geneva:

```{r}
districts_ge <- filter(dimensions, dimension == "GR_KT_GDE", parent == "GE")
communes_ge <- filter(dimensions, dimension == "GR_KT_GDE", parent %in% districts_ge$value)
communes_ge
```

You can use `communes_ge$value` in the filters. In the same way, `parent`
gives the total of a dimension, e.g. `_T` for all numbers of rooms.

The levels are not the same in all datasets: in some datasets, a commune
has no district. Check the parents of a few values first, as above.

The codes of the other dimensions:

```{r}
filter(dimensions, dimension != "GR_KT_GDE")
```

### Write the filters

The filters are a named list. The names are the dimensions, and the values
are the codes you want:

```{r}
filters <- list(
  GR_KT_GDE = c("GE", "ZH", "BE"), # the three cantons
  WOHN_ANZAHL = "_T",              # all numbers of rooms
  LEERWOHN_TYP = "_T",             # all types of vacant dwellings
  MEASURE_DIMENSION = "RATE"       # the vacancy rate, in %
)
```

A dimension that is not in the filters keeps all its values. If you make a
typo in the name of a dimension, you get an error. An empty vector of codes,
or `NA`, is also an error. So you never download all the data by mistake.

The API checks the codes. A code that does not exist gives no data. Some
values have no data, too. If no value of your query has data, you get the
error "No records found for the specified query.".

## Step 3: download the data

Download the vacancy rate since 2020 with the filters:

```{r}
rates <- bfs_sse_data(
  "DF_LWZ_1",
  filters = filters,
  start_period = "2020",
  language = "en"
)
rates
```

Put the three cantons side by side. Geneva has the lowest vacancy rate:

```{r}
rates |>
  select(GR_KT_GDE, TIME_PERIOD, value) |>
  tidyr::pivot_wider(names_from = GR_KT_GDE, values_from = value)
```

### The latest value

With `last_n = 1`, you get the last period of each series, without knowing
the year. The latest vacancy rate of the three cantons:

```{r}
bfs_sse_data(
  "DF_LWZ_1",
  filters = filters,
  last_n = 1,
  language = "en"
) |>
  select(GR_KT_GDE, TIME_PERIOD, value)
```

`last_n = 3` gives the last three periods, and `first_n` the first periods.
You can use them with `start_period` and `end_period`.

### The columns

- Two columns for each dimension: the codes (e.g. `GR_KT_GDE`) and the
  names (e.g. `GR_KT_GDE_label`). The column names are the dimension ids,
  in all languages.
- `TIME_PERIOD`: the period, e.g. the year.
- `value`: the number.

Other options:

- `labels = "code"` gives only the codes, and `labels = "label"` only the
  names. Be careful with `"label"`: two codes can have the same name (the
  canton and the city of Zurich), so use it only to show the data.
- `attributes = TRUE` adds information about each value, e.g.
  `OBS_STATUS` (for example, if the value is provisional). You get the codes
  and the names, as for the dimensions.

::: {.callout .callout-warning}
Without `filters`, `bfs_sse_data()` downloads all the data of the dataset.
This can be large and slow: some datasets have millions of values.
:::

### Dates

`TIME_PERIOD` is text, as the API gives it, for example `"2024"`,
`"2024-Q1"` or `"2024-01"`. For a plot, make a date from it. Download the
whole series since 1997 and make a date for each year:

```{r}
rates_all <- bfs_sse_data(
  "DF_LWZ_1",
  filters = filters,
  start_period = "1997",
  language = "en"
) |>
  mutate(date = as.Date(paste0(TIME_PERIOD, "-01-01")))
rates_all
```

Plot the vacancy rate of the three cantons:

```{r, eval = FALSE}
library(ggplot2)

ggplot(rates_all, aes(date, value, color = GR_KT_GDE_label)) +
  geom_line() +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "Vacancy rate (%)", color = NULL)
```

The year with the lowest vacancy rate in each canton:

```{r}
rates_all |>
  group_by(GR_KT_GDE) |>
  slice_min(value, n = 1) |>
  select(GR_KT_GDE, TIME_PERIOD, value)
```

## In a data pipeline

A dataset can have several versions. A new version can change the
dimensions, and your code can stop working. By default, the API uses the
latest version. To always get the same structure, set `version`:

```{r, eval = FALSE}
bfs_sse_data("DF_LWZ_1", filters = filters, version = "1.1.0")
```

`bfs_sse_datasets()` lists the versions of each dataset. On stats.swiss,
the version is in the URL of the query, e.g. `1.1.0` in
`CH1.LWZ,DF_LWZ_1,1.1.0`.

Each type of error has its own class, so you can handle it in your code:

- `bfs_no_records`: there is no data for your query.
- `bfs_sse_filter_error`: there is a problem with the filters.
- `bfs_sse_argument_error`: there is a problem with another argument.
- `bfs_sse_dataset_error`: the dataset or the version does not exist.
- `bfs_sse_query_error`: the API does not accept your query, e.g. a period
  in a wrong format or too many codes in the filters. The error gives the
  message of the API.
- `bfs_http_error`: the API is not available (see
  [API errors and rate limits](troubleshooting.html)).

## Moving from `bfs_get_sse_data()`

`bfs_get_sse_metadata()` and `bfs_get_sse_data()` are the old functions.
They are deprecated: they still work the same way, so your code does not
break, but they give a warning. To learn why
there are new functions and how to change your code, see
[Moving to the new Swiss Stats Explorer functions](sse-migration.html).
